analysis.one_liner: Bars a mortgage lender from starting foreclosure until it proves who owns the loan and the borrower was properly notified.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped lenders and servicers from starting a foreclosure until they filed a detailed report identifying who actually holds the mortgage note, confirming the loan was made and serviced lawfully, and stating whether the borrower was truly in default. It also required written notice to the homeowner at least five days before foreclosure began, listing amounts owed, deadlines, rights, and modification options. The report had to be prepared by an independent party with no stake in the foreclosure. It applied to owner-occupied homes of one to four units.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure on their primary residences. They would learn who actually owns their loan — a frequent sticking point after loans were bundled and resold during the housing boom — get documented proof that required notices were sent, and receive an itemized statement of what they owed and what options, such as modification, were available. If a loan was made or serviced illegally, the report could support a defense or extended redemption period.

how_it_helps.text: Before any foreclosure could begin, the foreclosing party had to file a report from an independent party identifying the actual holder of the mortgage note, the originating lender, and every subsequent assignee, plus anyone who received federal bailout assistance tied to the mortgage [S3].

The report had to state whether the loan was made and serviced in compliance with major consumer protection laws, whether a bona fide default actually occurred, and whether misrepresentations fraudulently induced the borrower, with findings that could support extended rights to rescind or redeem the home [S3].

The foreclosing party had to give the homeowner written notice at least five days before starting the foreclosure, listing amounts in arrears and fees itemized, deadlines for raising defenses, consequences of not responding, and workout or modification options [S3].
The notice had to include correct contact information and state licensing numbers for the mortgage holder and servicer, so borrowers could reach the parties actually deciding their case [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and investors holding mortgage notes. Preparing an independent compliance report on every covered foreclosure — covering ten federal statutes plus state law — would add cost and time to each case, and delays in foreclosure can extend the period a loan sits in default. Some of that cost would flow into servicing and lending costs generally. Foreclosure law firms and document processing vendors would also lose routine business built on less rigorous filings.

drawbacks.text: The compliance report requirement was broad: an independent party would have to certify compliance with ten federal statutes and all applicable state and local lending law for every foreclosure, a review with no clear industry infrastructure or defined standard, which could substantially delay or raise the cost of foreclosures, including legitimate ones [S3].

The bill preempted state foreclosure procedures where inconsistent, a federal override of a field traditionally governed by state law, though it preserved state rules that offer stronger protections [S3].
Slower foreclosures extend the time a property sits in default, which can worsen the condition of homes and the surrounding neighborhood and increase losses that get priced into future lending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Coming right after the robo-signing scandal, when courts found foreclosures filed with unverified or false loan documents, the core idea — prove you own the note and follow the law before taking someone's home — addressed a real, documented failure. But the bill went beyond that with a sweeping independent-report requirement covering every consumer statute on the books, which made it heavier than the problem demanded and easy for critics to portray as a near-moratorium. A narrower version requiring proof of note ownership and proper notice likely would have been more politically viable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on April 15, 2011, joined by Rep. John Conyers [S1].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1].
On May 2, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and to the Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity [S5].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and lenders facing foreclosure documentation requirements are better off, since the bill never advanced and no comparable federal requirement became law during that Congress.

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Produce the Note Act of 2011 in the House.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had two Democratic sponsors and no recorded opposition, so the partisan shape is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to prove loan ownership, legal compliance, and proper notice before foreclosing on a primary residence, adding cost, delay, and litigation exposure to their foreclosure operations. Borrowers would gain verification of exactly what the industry had been able to assert without independent documentation.

industries.industry: Foreclosure law firms and document processing vendors
industries.note: Firms whose business rested on high-volume foreclosure filings would face an independent-report requirement for each case, disrupting the streamlined pipeline that came under scrutiny during the robo-signing scandal.

Because loans were often transferred multiple times, investors would face scrutiny of the chain of ownership; if a loan was found noncompliant, extended rescission or redemption rights could reduce recoveries on defaulted loans.
